name: Composite bonding

lead: Composite bonding is a dental procedure in which a dentist applies a tooth-coloured resin and hardens it with a blue curing light so that it bonds to the tooth, improving appearance. It is used to repair cracks or close gaps, and is one of the options for masking chips and stains.
Adhesive dentistry began with Michael Buonocore's 1955 acid-etching work, and Irwin Smigel helped popularise cosmetic uses such as closing gaps and recontouring in place of crowns.

paras: Enamel and dentin are treated with a bonding agent, and the resin is then applied and cured. Bonding agents have moved from total-etch systems (fourth and fifth generation) to self-etch (sixth and seventh) and universal adhesives introduced in 2012, which are said to bond to several substrates.

Wikipedia says the best longevity came from fourth-generation, multi-step agents, and that simpler self-etch systems were more convenient. Registered trials compare bonding agents mainly for post-operative sensitivity and restoration performance in non-carious cervical lesions.

lead: Composite bonding, also called dental bonding, is the attachment of a tooth-coloured resin to natural enamel and dentin; the dentist applies the resin and cures it with visible blue light so it bonds to the tooth and improves its appearance [1]. Direct composite bonding is used to repair cracks or gaps [1].

Bonding is part of adhesive dentistry, which has been used in operative, preventive, cosmetic, paediatric and prosthodontic dentistry and in orthodontics, where it attaches brackets [1]. Wikipedia dates adhesive dentistry to Michael Buonocore's 1955 acid-etching paper, and credits Irwin Smigel with broadening its use to close gaps and recontour teeth rather than use crowns [1].

Published research is mostly about adhesives and restorative composites in general, such as lab bond-strength testing, rather than the cosmetic masking of stains and chips specifically [2][3]. No studies of cosmetic composite bonding as such were located.

paras: Wikipedia traces bonding agents from no-etch to total-etch (fourth and fifth generation) and then to self-etch systems (sixth and seventh generation), which reduced sensitivity to operator error. Universal adhesives, introduced in 2012, are said to bond to enamel, dentin, metal, porcelain, ceramic and zirconia in a single application, though the term has no settled definition [1].

A review of restorative composites reports that nanofiller particles enhance the properties of various reinforced composites, including mechanical strength and physical properties [3]. A guidance paper from the Academy of Dental Materials addresses in vitro micro-tensile bond strength testing of dental adhesives to enamel and dentin [4].

The Wikipedia article says the best bonding and longevity came from fourth-generation agents, which use separate etch, prime and bond steps, but gives no other durability figures [1]. It also cites a Cochrane review finding no clear evidence for choosing one orthodontic adhesive over another [1].

No studies found of composite bonding specifically for masking stains and chips for cosmetic purposes. Registered trials involve related adhesive questions, such as comparing fifth- and eighth-generation bonding agents for post-operative sensitivity in class I restorations [5], clinical evaluation of a two-step universal adhesive in non-carious cervical lesions [6], and comparison of adhesive systems containing HEMA and 10-MDP in such lesions [7]. A further registered trial examines tooth discoloration and handling time of flowable versus packable composites for clear aligner attachments [8].

timeline.event: Michael Buonocore publishes the acid-etching paper that began adhesive dentistry.[1]
Irwin Smigel publishes a guide to aesthetic dentistry.[1]
